name: Oxymetazoline cream (Rhofade)

card.summary: A prescription vasoconstrictor cream approved in 2017 for persistent facial redness of rosacea; it narrows vessels for a temporary reduction in redness.
card.note: Prescription-only in the US; effect lasts only while applied, and the same drug in nasal sprays is known for rebound congestion.

quick.overview:
Rhofade is a 1% oxymetazoline cream that the FDA approved in January 2017 for persistent facial redness (erythema) in adults with rosacea. Oxymetazoline is the same decongestant ingredient found in nasal sprays such as Afrin.

It is discussed in skincare circles as a temporary redness reducer that works by shrinking blood vessels in the skin. It is a prescription product in the US; reviews in prescribing journals evaluated its approval.
quick.mechanism: Oxymetazoline is a direct-acting sympathomimetic that mainly activates alpha-1 and, to a lesser degree, alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, narrowing small blood vessels. In the skin this reduces visible redness while the drug is present.
quick.risks: The nasal-spray form is known for rebound congestion with prolonged use. For the cream, prescribing reviews describe local skin reactions as the main adverse effects; consult the label for full details. It is prescription-only in the US.

lead: Oxymetazoline cream (brand name Rhofade) is a topical 1% formulation of the alpha-adrenergic agonist oxymetazoline, approved by the US FDA in January 2017 for persistent facial erythema associated with rosacea in adults [4][1]. It is a vasoconstrictor intended to reduce visible redness [4].

Oxymetazoline itself is an older drug developed by Merck in 1961 and sold as a nasal decongestant [4]. The cream was reviewed in drug-approval summaries for primary care [2] and in The Medical Letter [3]. A bioequivalence study in rosacea enrolled 1,105 participants [5].

paras: The approved indication is persistent facial redness associated with rosacea in adults [1][4]. Rosacea overviews list oxymetazoline alongside brimonidine as vasoconstrictor topicals, with less detailed evidence for oxymetazoline in that reference [6].

Oxymetazoline is an imidazole derivative and direct-acting sympathomimetic that mainly activates alpha-1 adrenergic receptors and, to a lesser extent, alpha-2 receptors, narrowing blood vessels [4]. Merck developed it from xylometazoline in 1961, and the Afrin nasal spray reached over-the-counter status in 1975 [4].

A review of the nasal spray found that use beyond about three days can cause rebound congestion [4]. For the cream, safety and tolerability with laser or energy-based therapy was studied in a 46-person phase 4 trial [7]. Readers are referred to the product label and the cited reviews [1][3] for the full adverse-effect profile.

Evidence summaries for the cream are published in American Family Physician [1] and The Medical Letter [3]. Registered studies include a 1,105-participant clinical-endpoint bioequivalence trial [5] and a 46-person phase 4 study of oxymetazoline with energy-based therapy in rosacea [7]. Detailed efficacy figures are not reproduced here.
The cream is discussed as a temporary option for facial redness, in the same breath as brimonidine gel and in-clinic vascular lasers.

timeline.event: Afrin nasal spray becomes available over the counter. [4]
FDA approves oxymetazoline 1% cream (Rhofade) for facial redness of rosacea. [4][2]
